claim: tRNA structure and nucleotide modifications can each interfere with cDNA synthesis by commonly used reverse transcriptases (RTs).
source: Among the major classes of RNAs in the cell, tRNAs remain the most difficult to characterize via deep sequencing approaches, as tRNA structure and nucleotide modifications can each interfere with cDNA synthesis by commonly used reverse transcriptases (RTs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field, supported by the context of the manuscript and references to prior work.

claim: OTTR successfully captures both full-length tRNAs and tRNA fragments in budding yeast and in mouse reproductive tissues without any prior enzymatic treatment.
source: We show that OTTR successfully captures both full-length tRNAs and tRNA fragments in budding yeast and in mouse reproductive tissues without any prior enzymatic treatment, and that tRNA cloning efficiency can be further enhanced via AlkB-mediated demethylation of modified nucleotides.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing tRNA capture in various samples.

claim: tRNA cloning efficiency can be further enhanced via AlkB-mediated demethylation of modified nucleotides.
source: We show that OTTR successfully captures both full-length tRNAs and tRNA fragments in budding yeast and in mouse reproductive tissues without any prior enzymatic treatment, and that tRNA cloning efficiency can be further enhanced via AlkB-mediated demethylation of modified nucleotides.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing AlkB-treated and untreated samples (Figure 5).

claim: A subset of nucleotide modifications leave misincorporation signatures in OTTR datasets.
source: As with other recent tRNA cloning protocols, we find that a subset of nucleotide modifications leave misincorporation signatures in OTTR datasets, enabling their detection without any additional protocol steps.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data in Figure 2 showing mismatches at known modification sites.

claim: OTTR provides the most accurate picture of tRNA fragment levels by comparison to 'ground truth' Northern blots.
source: Focusing on tRNA cleavage products, we compare OTTR with several standard small RNA-Seq protocols, finding that OTTR provides the most accurate picture of tRNA fragment levels by comparison to 'ground truth' Northern blots.
evidence: This is supported by comparison data in Figure 3 showing OTTR results match Northern blot validation better than other protocols.

claim: Mature mouse spermatozoa contain a far more complex population of tRNA fragments – including both 5′ and 3′ tRNA halves derived from the majority of tRNAs – than previously appreciated.
source: Applying this protocol to mature mouse spermatozoa, our data dramatically alter our understanding of the small RNA cargo of mature mammalian sperm, revealing a far more complex population of tRNA fragments – including both 5′ and 3′ tRNA halves derived from the majority of tRNAs – than previously appreciated.
evidence: This is supported by OTTR sequencing data from mouse sperm shown in Figure 4.

claim: The cellular repertoire of tRNAs differs between different cell types.
source: Nonetheless, there is increasing evidence that the cellular repertoire of tRNAs differs between different cell types, and within a given cell type can be shaped by external factors from proliferation rate (Gingold et al., 2014; Hernandez-Alias et al., 2020) to metabolite levels (Laxman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mature tRNAs are cleaved in response to cellular stressors.
source: Mature tRNAs are also cleaved in response to cellular stressors (Lee and Collins, 2005; Lee et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 2008; Yamasaki et al., 2009), and the resulting cleavage products – broadly known as tRNA fragments, or tRFs – are increasingly appreciated as potential regulatory molecules in their own right (Anderson and Ivanov, 2014; Keam and Hutvagner, 2015; Su et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: tRNA fragments (tRFs) are increasingly appreciated as potential regulatory molecules.
source: Mature tRNAs are also cleaved in response to cellular stressors (Lee and Collins, 2005; Lee et al., 2009; Thompson et al., 2008; Yamasaki et al., 2009), and the resulting cleavage products – broadly known as tRNA fragments, or tRFs – are increasingly appreciated as potential regulatory molecules in their own right (Anderson and Ivanov, 2014; Keam and Hutvagner, 2015; Su et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some ~15–20% of all tRNA nucleotides are covalently modified.
source: tRNAs are subject to a wide range of covalent nucleotide modifications, with some ~15–20% of all tRNA nucleotides thought to be covalently modified to form species ranging from 5-methylcytosine and pseudouridine to more complex modifications like wybutosine or methoxy-carbonyl-methyl-thiouridine (Phizicky and Hopper, 2010; Phizicky and Hopper, 2015; Pan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: N1-methylguanosine (m1G), N1-methyladenosine (m1A), N3-methylcytosine (m3C), and N2,N2-dimethylguanosine (m22G) interfere with commonly used reverse transcriptases (RTs) and prevent the synthesis of full-length cDNAs.
source: Several of these modifications, particularly N1-methylguanosine (m1G), N1-methyladenosine (m1A), N3-methylcytosine (m3C), and N2,N2-dimethylguanosine (m22G), are known to interfere with commonly used reverse transcriptases (RTs) and prevent the synthesis of full-length cDNAs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Systematic analyses of intact tRNA levels typically relied on microarray hybridization to avoid a requirement for reverse transcription.
source: As a result, until recently, systematic analyses of intact tRNA levels typically relied on microarray hybridization (Dittmar et al., 2006; Dittmar et al., 2004) to avoid a requirement for reverse transcription.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work using microarray approaches.

claim: Typical deep sequencing efforts capture only a subset of the tRFs in a given sample.
source: With respect to tRFs, although typical deep sequencing efforts do capture some tRNA cleavage products, they are clearly limited to only a subset of the tRFs in a given sample.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that Northern blots show tRFs not captured by typical protocols.

claim: Most studies of mammalian sperm have documented very high levels of 5′ fragments of a small handful of tRNAs (most notably including Gly-GCC, Glu-CTC, and Val-CAC).
source: For instance, a large number of groups have characterized small (18–40 nt) RNAs in mammalian sperm, with most such studies documenting very high levels of 5′ fragments of a small handful of tRNAs (most notably including Gly-GCC, Glu-CTC, and Val-CAC).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of findings from multiple published studies.

claim: Northern blots show that 3′ tRNA fragments are present in mammalian sperm samples but are not captured by typical commercial library preparation protocols such as Illumina TruSeq.
source: Yet Northern blots show that 3′ tRNA fragments are also present in these samples (Sharma et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018,) but are not captured by typical commercial library preparation protocols such as Illumina TruSeq.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published Northern blot data.

claim: Hydro-tRNAseq introduced limited hydrolysis of full-length tRNAs to yield short fragments for cloning and sequencing.
source: For instance, to reduce barriers to reverse transcription caused by secondary structures, Hydro-tRNAseq introduced limited hydrolysis of full-length tRNAs to yield short fragments for cloning and sequencing (Karaca et al., 2014; Gogakos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the Hydro-tRNAseq publications.

claim: Several early protocols leveraged the highly processive thermostable group II intron reverse transcriptase (TGIRT) to overcome tRNA secondary structures.
source: Alternatively, several early protocols leveraged the highly processive thermostable group II intron reverse transcriptase (TGIRT) to overcome tRNA secondary structures (Mohr et al., 2013), along with enzymatic demethylation of m1G, m1A, and m3C by bacterial AlkB in an attempt to avoid premature RT termination (Zheng et al., 2015; Cozen et al., 2015; Dai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published protocols.

claim: mim-tRNAseq efficiently captures full-length tRNAs with only modest levels of premature RT termination.
source: Although these first-generation protocols yielded few full-length tRNA sequences, a substantially improved TGIRT-based protocol – mim-tRNAseq – was recently shown to efficiently capture full-length tRNAs with only modest levels of premature RT termination (Behrens et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the mim-tRNAseq publication.

claim: YAMAT-seq, LOTTE-seq, nano-tRNAseq, and QuantM-seq rely on adaptor ligation to the 3' CCA on the tRNA acceptor stem and are thus suitable for intact tRNA cloning but cannot be used for analysis of tRNA fragments.
source: For instance, many of the methods mentioned above – YAMAT-seq, nano-tRNAseq, LOTTE-seq, and QuantM-seq – rely on adaptor ligation to the 3' CCA on the tRNA acceptor stem and are thus suitable for intact tRNA cloning but cannot be used for analysis of tRNA fragments.
evidence: This is based on the authors' understanding of the published protocols.

claim: OTTR exploits an engineered version of the Bombyx mori R2 retroelement reverse transcriptase for sequential template jumping.
source: To capture an accurate profile of small RNAs with well-defined RNA 5′ and 3′ ends, a novel protocol was developed – Ordered Two-Template Relay, or OTTR (Upton et al., 2021) – that exploits an engineered version of the Bombyx mori R2 retroelement reverse transcriptase (Bibiłło and Eickbush, 2002) for sequential template jumping.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the OTTR publication.

claim: In a one-step RT reaction, OTTR joins 5′ and 3′ adaptors to a full-length cDNA copy of input RNA.
source: In a one-step RT reaction, OTTR joins 5′ and 3′ adaptors to a full-length cDNA copy of input RNA.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the OTTR protocol.

claim: Benchmarking a large number of protocols for bias in the capture of a defined mixture of synthetic small RNAs revealed significantly lower bias for OTTR than for any commercial protocol.
source: Benchmarking a large number of protocols for bias in the capture of a defined mixture of synthetic small RNAs revealed significantly lower bias for OTTR than for any commercial protocol (Upton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the OTTR benchmarking publication.

claim: Characterization of RNA in tissue culture cell lines using OTTR captured substantial levels of intact tRNAs.
source: Intriguingly, characterization of RNA in tissue culture cell lines using OTTR captured substantial levels of intact tRNAs, suggesting that OTTR could be a promising protocol for tRNA sequencing applications.
evidence: This is based on data from the OTTR publication.

claim: More full-length tRNAs were recovered when using the more lenient RNA sizing by mirVana spin column compared to gel-mediated size selection.
source: Surprisingly, we consistently recovered more full-length tRNAs when using the more lenient RNA sizing by mirVana spin column (Figure 1A), suggesting that the process of gel-mediated size selection likely results in tRNA fragmentation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A comparing the two methods.

claim: The process of gel-mediated size selection likely results in tRNA fragmentation.
source: Surprisingly, we consistently recovered more full-length tRNAs when using the more lenient RNA sizing by mirVana spin column (Figure 1A), suggesting that the process of gel-mediated size selection likely results in tRNA fragmentation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that gel purification yields fewer full-length tRNAs.

claim: The majority (~70–90% of reads) of tRNAs were full length in both mouse and yeast samples using OTTR.
source: For each tRNA, we calculated the percentage of full-length reads, finding that the majority (~70–90% of reads) of tRNAs were full length in both mouse and yeast samples (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: YAMAT-seq was the most efficient protocol for intact tRNA capture, with reads almost completely derived from full length tRNAs.
source: Comparison to a range of prior tRNA sequencing datasets (Gogakos et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2015; Cozen et al., 2015; Behrens et al., 2021; Shigematsu et al., 2017; Erber et al., 2020; Pinkard et al., 2020; Scacchetti et al., 2024; Watkins et al., 2022; Scheepbouwer et al., 2023) revealed that YAMAT-seq was the most efficient protocol for intact tRNA capture, with reads almost completely derived from full length tRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of multiple published datasets shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: YAMAT-seq data were very low complexity, with two tRNAs (Lys-CTT, Glu-GTC) representing 82–86% of all tRNA mapping reads across all three cell lines analyzed.
source: That said, YAMAT-seq data were very low complexity, with two tRNAs (Lys-CTT, Glu-GTC) representing 82–86% of all tRNA mapping reads across all three cell lines analyzed (not shown).
evidence: This is based on analysis of YAMAT-seq data by the authors.

claim: OTTR and mim-tRNAseq were comparable in terms of capturing full-length tRNAs with ~70–90% of tRNA-mapping reads representing full-length sequences.
source: After YAMAT-seq, OTTR and mim-tRNAseq (Behrens et al., 2021) were comparable in terms of capturing full-length tRNAs with ~70–90% of tRNA-mapping reads representing full-length sequences, while the remaining protocols captured various types of partial tRNAs potentially attributable to premature RT termination, internal RT priming, or other forms of tRNA degradation or breakage (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is good overall quantitative agreement between intact tRNA levels measured by OTTR and datasets from comparable samples.
source: Moreover, we find good overall quantitative agreement between intact tRNA levels measured by OTTR and datasets from comparable samples (e.g. actively growing yeast, and mouse testis), including a dataset obtained using the Nanopore-based nano-tRNAseq (Lucas et al., 2024) protocol (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: mim-tRNAseq exhibited the best performance (R=0.96) in capturing the known correspondence between tRNA gene copy number and tRNA abundance.
source: Finally, we explored the ability of these various protocols to capture the known correspondence between tRNA gene copy number and tRNA abundance, with mim-tRNAseq exhibiting the best performance (R=0.96), followed by OTTR (R=0.5–0.7 across datasets), followed by ARM-seq, Lotte, and nano-tRNAseq (R=0.4–0.5 for all three protocols).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of tRNA levels vs gene copy number.

claim: Known nucleotide modification sites, including the common m1G modification found at position 9 of many tRNAs, could be barriers to reverse transcription.
source: Visualization of sequence coverage and read start and stop locations for several tRNAs (Figure 1D) suggested that known nucleotide modification sites, including the common m1G modification found at position 9 of many tRNAs (eg, tRNA-Ile-AAT), could be barriers to reverse transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from coverage plots showing reduced coverage at modification sites (Figure 1D).

claim: Further gains in the efficiency of full-length tRNA capture were observed in trm1Δ yeast lacking m22G.
source: To directly test whether premature termination is affected by nucleotide modifications, we prepared full-length tRNA libraries from trm1Δ yeast lacking the methylase responsible for m22G (Hopper et al., 1982). We find further gains in the efficiency of full-length tRNA capture in this strain background (Figure 1E and F), suggesting that this nucleotide modification presents a partial barrier to reverse transcription (see below).
evidence: This is supported by data comparing WT and trm1Δ yeast shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The m22G nucleotide modification presents a partial barrier to reverse transcription.
source: To directly test whether premature termination is affected by nucleotide modifications, we prepared full-length tRNA libraries from trm1Δ yeast lacking the methylase responsible for m22G (Hopper et al., 1982). We find further gains in the efficiency of full-length tRNA capture in this strain background (Figure 1E and F), suggesting that this nucleotide modification presents a partial barrier to reverse transcription (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from improved tRNA capture in trm1Δ yeast.

claim: Many nucleotide modifications in tRNAs involve chemical alterations that affect the pattern of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors at the base pairing interface.
source: Many of the nucleotide modifications in tRNAs involve chemical alterations that affect the pattern of hydrogen bond donors and acceptors at the base pairing interface.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about tRNA modifications.

claim: 'Incorrect' nucleotides can be incorporated into cDNA at modified positions during reverse transcription, resulting in a 'mutation/misincorporation' signature for modified nucleotides in deep sequencing data.
source: As a result, 'incorrect' nucleotides (relative to those expected from tRNA genomic sequences) can be incorporated into cDNA at these positions during the process of reverse transcription, resulting in a 'mutation/misincorporation' signature for modified nucleotides in deep sequencing data.
evidence: This is stated as a known consequence of tRNA modifications during sequencing.

claim: Examination of individual yeast tRNAs revealed high levels of misincorporation at multiple positions throughout the tRNA, with mismatches localized at various known modification sites, including m1G, m22G, m3C, and m1A nucleotides.
source: Examination of individual yeast tRNAs revealed high levels of misincorporation at multiple positions throughout the tRNA (Figure 2A), with mismatches localized at various known modification sites, including the expected mismatches at m1G, m22G, m3C, and m1A nucleotides.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Examination of the same tRNA species in trm1Δ dataset revealed the expected loss of nucleotide misincorporation at G26.
source: Examination of the same tRNA species in our trm1Δ dataset revealed the expected loss of nucleotide misincorporation at G26 in this mutant (Figure 2B), confirming that the m22G nucleotide modification is responsible for the mutational signature at this position.
evidence: This is supported by data comparing WT and trm1Δ shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The m22G nucleotide modification is responsible for the mutational signature at position 26.
source: Examination of the same tRNA species in our trm1Δ dataset revealed the expected loss of nucleotide misincorporation at G26 in this mutant (Figure 2B), confirming that the m22G nucleotide modification is responsible for the mutational signature at this position.
evidence: This is confirmed by loss of the signature in trm1Δ mutant.

claim: High levels of misincorporation were observed at tRNA positions 9, 26, and 58, corresponding to well-known locations of m1G, m22G, and m1A, respectively.
source: Consistent with prior observations (Behrens et al., 2021; Pinkard et al., 2020), we observed high levels of misincorporation at tRNA positions 9, 26, and 58, corresponding to well-known locations of m1G, m22G, and m1A, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2C-E and citations to prior work.

claim: The mutational signature at position 26 is completely lost in the trm1Δ background.
source: Moreover, as seen for individual tRNAs (Figure 2B, red arrows), we find that the mutational signature at position 26 is completely lost in the trm1Δ background (Figure 2D, red arrow), confirming the causal link between the m22G modification and the misincorporation signature at this position.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mismatches were only observed in the subset of tRNAs known to be modified at the position in question.
source: Closer examination of the specific tRNA species exhibiting mismatches at any given position in yeast (Figure 2F) confirmed that mismatches were only observed in the subset of tRNAs known to be modified at the position in question (Dunin-Horkawicz et al., 2006), as for example alanine tRNAs carry m1G at position 9 whereas histidine tRNAs do not (Figure 2F, leftmost panel).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2F and citation to the MODOMICS database.

claim: Several locations were associated with sequencing mismatches including known locations for 3-methylcytidine (32), inosine and 1-methylinosine (34 and 37), and wybutosine (37).
source: Beyond the mutational signature observed at known locations of m22G, m1G, and m1A, several other locations were associated with sequencing mismatches (Figure 2C and F). These included known locations for 3-methylcytidine (32), inosine and 1-methylinosine (34 and 37), and wybutosine (37), as well as lower frequency of misincorporation at several locations currently annotated as unmodified nucleotides in the MODOMICS database (Dunin-Horkawicz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2C and F.

claim: Budding yeast do not encode any RNase A or L family members, and encode a single RNase T2 family member, RNY1p.
source: Cellular tRNAs can be cleaved by a number of different nucleases, including RNase A, T, and L family members, in a variety of species (Lee and Collins, 2005; Thompson et al., 2008; Yamasaki et al., 2009; Thompson and Parker, 2009; Andersen and Collins, 2012). Conveniently, budding yeast do not encode any RNase A or L family members, and encode a single RNase T2 family member, RNY1p.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about yeast nucleases, supported by citations.

claim: RNY1p overexpression has been reported to drive high levels of tRNA cleavage.
source: As RNY1p overexpression has previously been reported to drive high levels of tRNA cleavage (Thompson and Parker, 2009), we generated a construct bearing RNY1 under the control of the galactose-inducible pGAL1-10 promoter.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Overexpression of RNY1p leads to high levels of tRNA-Gly-GCC cleavage.
source: We confirmed by Northern blot analysis that overexpression of RNY1p lead to high levels of tRNA-Gly-GCC cleavage in our hands (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), providing a convenient system for the production of high levels of tRNA fragments for benchmarking small RNA cloning protocols.
evidence: This is supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All three protocols (TruSeq, NEBNext, OTTR) captured tRFs of similar lengths, albeit with moderate differences between the three protocols.
source: All three protocols captured tRFs of similar lengths, albeit with moderate differences between the three protocols – NEBNext was a particular outlier in this regard, with peaks of read counts for specific tRF lengths that were far more prominent in these libraries than in libraries made with the other two protocols.
evidence: This is based on comparison of size distributions in Figure 3B.

claim: NEBNext exhibited peaks of read counts for specific tRF lengths that were far more prominent than in libraries made with the other two protocols.
source: All three protocols captured tRFs of similar lengths, albeit with moderate differences between the three protocols – NEBNext was a particular outlier in this regard, with peaks of read counts for specific tRF lengths that were far more prominent in these libraries than in libraries made with the other two protocols.
evidence: This is observed in the size distribution data.

claim: Relatively few distinct tRNA fragments were captured using the NEB protocol, contrasting with the far wider range of tRFs captured using the Fu2018 protocol and OTTR.
source: As shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, we captured relatively few distinct tRNA fragments using the NEB protocol, contrasting with the far wider range of tRFs captured using the Fu2018 protocol and OTTR.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: OTTR revealed the greatest diversity of tRFs of all the protocols examined.
source: Overall, we find that OTTR revealed the greatest diversity of tRFs of all the protocols examined.
evidence: This is based on comparison of tRF diversity across protocols.

claim: OTTR datasets exhibited the greatest complexity in the range of tRNA fragments captured.
source: This analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) again reveals remarkably few tRNA species efficiently captured by NEBNext, contrasting with somewhat better tRNA capture using the Fu et al., 2018 protocol, with our OTTR datasets exhibiting the greatest complexity in the range of tRNA fragments captured.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The relatively even representation of yeast tRNA species, and 5′ and 3′ halves, is consistent with the expectation that RNase T2 family members like RNY1p should have only modest sequence preferences.
source: The relatively even representation of yeast tRNA species, and 5′ and 3′ halves, is consistent with the expectation that RNase T2 family members like RNY1p should have only modest sequence preferences beyond a preference for pyrimidines present in single-stranded RNA loop regions, and should therefore cleave most tRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and knowledge of RNase T2 specificity.

claim: All three protocols robustly captured the 3′ half of tRNA-Gly-GCC, but OTTR uniquely captured the 5′ fragments of this tRNA that were absent from the other two libraries.
source: For example, although all three protocols robustly captured the 3′ half of tRNA-Gly-GCC, OTTR uniquely captured the 5′ fragments of this tRNA that were absent from the other two libraries (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by coverage data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: For the two tRNAs for which the different deep sequencing protocols showed substantial differences in tRNA coverage, OTTR more faithfully captured the tRNA fragment ratio detected by Northern blots.
source: To validate these protocols by comparison to an independent ground truth, we assayed the 5′ and 3′ halves of four tRNAs by Northern blotting (Figure 3D and E, right panels, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2). For the two tRNAs for which the different deep sequencing protocols showed substantial differences in tRNA coverage, OTTR more faithfully captured the tRNA fragment ratio detected by Northern blots.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of sequencing data to Northern blots in Figure 3D and E.

claim: OTTR captures a wider range of tRNA fragments, more even levels of 5′ and 3′ tRNA halves, and better agrees with ground truth Northern blots.
source: Taken together, our data show that OTTR captures a wider range of tRNA fragments, more even levels of 5′ and 3′ tRNA halves, and better agrees with ground truth Northern blots, all of which strongly support the utility of OTTR for analysis of tRNA-derived small RNAs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the yeast tRF experiments.

claim: Scores of studies over the past decade have documented abundant tRNA fragments in mammalian sperm, with the majority of published datasets documenting highly abundant 5′ tRFs.
source: Scores of studies over the past decade have documented abundant tRNA fragments in mammalian sperm, with the majority of published datasets documenting highly abundant 5′ tRFs, with the 5′ halves of tRNA-Glu-CTC, tRNA-Val-CAC, and tRNA-Gly-GCC representing the three most abundant tRFs in mouse sperm (Peng et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Standard deep sequencing analyses are insufficient to fully capture the sperm RNA payload.
source: However, it has been clear for years that standard deep sequencing analyses are insufficient to fully capture the sperm RNA payload.
evidence: This is stated based on prior observations in the field.

claim: RNA cleavage by RNase A, T, or L family members is known to leave RNA 3′ ends bearing a cyclic 2′–3′ phosphate.
source: First, RNA cleavage by RNase A, T, or L family members is known to leave RNA 3′ ends bearing a cyclic 2′–3′ phosphate (which can spontaneously resolve to 2′- or 3′-phosphorylated ends), a modification that prevents RNA ligation during cloning.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about RNase cleavage products.

claim: Resolving cyclic 2′–3′ phosphates via T4 Polynucleotide Kinase (PNK) treatment resulted in a dramatic shift in captured sperm RNAs.
source: Indeed, resolving cyclic 2′–3′ phosphates via T4 Polynucleotide Kinase (PNK) treatment (Honda et al., 2015) resulted a dramatic shift in captured sperm RNAs (Sharma et al., 2018), revealing a far greater abundance and diversity of rRNA cleavage products than previously appreciated, along with longer 5′ tRFs that presumably reflect the primary cleavage site for reproductive tract nucleases (see below).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Northern blotting studies in sperm and epididymis samples revealed the presence of 3′ tRNA halves that are not represented in deep sequencing datasets.
source: In addition, Northern blotting studies in sperm and epididymis samples revealed the presence of 3′ tRNA halves that are not represented in deep sequencing datasets (Sharma et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018), further emphasizing our incomplete understanding of the mammalian sperm RNA payload.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published Northern blot studies.

claim: PNK treatment (with or without ATP) resulted in a substantial increase in capture of rRNA-derived fragments in ligation-based cloning methods.
source: Focusing first on the ligation-based cloning methods, we confirm prior reports (Sharma et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021) showing that PNK treatment (with or without ATP) resulted in a substantial increase in capture of rRNA-derived fragments (Figure 4B), consistent with the hypothesis that rRNA fragments in mammalian sperm are generated by a nuclease of the RNase A, T, or L families.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and citations to prior work.

claim: rRNA fragments in mammalian sperm are generated by a nuclease of the RNase A, T, or L families.
source: Focusing first on the ligation-based cloning methods, we confirm prior reports (Sharma et al., 2018; Shi et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021) showing that PNK treatment (with or without ATP) resulted in a substantial increase in capture of rRNA-derived fragments (Figure 4B), consistent with the hypothesis that rRNA fragments in mammalian sperm are generated by a nuclease of the RNase A, T, or L families.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of PNK treatment on rRNA fragment capture.

claim: The composition of OTTR libraries was far less dependent on PNK treatment compared to the ligation-based small RNA-Seq libraries.
source: Compared to the ligation-based small RNA-Seq libraries, the composition of OTTR libraries was far less dependent on PNK treatment (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data in Figure 4B.

claim: Many of the tRNA fragments that required PNK treatment for capture in TruSeq or NEB libraries were already abundant in untreated OTTR libraries and unaffected by PNK treatment.
source: Many of the tRNA fragments that required PNK treatment for capture in TruSeq or NEB libraries were already abundant in untreated OTTR libraries and unaffected by PNK treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PNK treatment led to improved capture of a subset of tRFs in OTTR libraries.
source: Nonetheless, PNK treatment did lead to improved capture of a subset of tRFs in OTTR libraries (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), and close examination of 3′ cleavage sites revealed capture of longer species for some 5′ tRFs (see for example Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, red arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Although OTTR appears to be able to capture small RNAs bearing 3′ phosphates and/or 2′–3′ cyclic phosphate moieties, PNK treatment nonetheless enhances capture of some RNA cleavage products by this protocol.
source: Taken together, our findings demonstrate that although OTTR appears to be able to capture small RNAs bearing 3′ phosphates and/or 2′–3′ cyclic phosphate moieties, PNK treatment nonetheless enhances capture of some RNA cleavage products by this protocol and thus should be included for quantitative analyses of tRNA and rRNA cleavage products.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PNK treatment experiments.

claim: Nucleotide modifications are generally thought to be a major reason for the historical difficulty of cloning intact tRNAs.
source: In addition to 3′ end chemistry, a number of common nucleotide modifications in tRNAs are well known to interfere with typically used RTs; indeed, these modifications are generally thought to be a major reason for the historical difficulty of cloning intact tRNAs (Zheng et al., 2015; Cozen et al., 2015; Dai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The improved capture of full-length tRNAs in trm1Δ yeast suggested that nucleotide modifications might impede R2 RT under at least some OTTR library preparation conditions.
source: Although the baseline OTTR protocol successfully captures tRNAs and tRNA fragments without any enzymatic pretreatment, the improved capture of full-length tRNAs in trm1Δ yeast (Figure 1E and F) suggested that nucleotide modifications might nonetheless impede R2 RT under at least some OTTR library preparation conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the trm1Δ data in Figure 1E and F.

claim: AlkB treatment removes m1A and m3C, as assessed by the near-complete loss of nucleotide mismatches at the relevant positions.
source: Focusing first on full-length tRNAs, we confirm that AlkB treatment removes m1A and m3C, as assessed by the near-complete loss of nucleotide mismatches at the relevant positions, but had little to no effect on m1G or m22G (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5A showing loss of mismatches after AlkB treatment.

claim: AlkB treatment had little to no effect on m1G or m22G.
source: Focusing first on full-length tRNAs, we confirm that AlkB treatment removes m1A and m3C, as assessed by the near-complete loss of nucleotide mismatches at the relevant positions, but had little to no effect on m1G or m22G (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5A showing persistent mismatches at these positions after AlkB treatment.

claim: Modest changes in intact tRNA capture were found following AlkB demethylation, with up to ~threefold altered levels of capture of a variety of tRNAs in the mouse system.
source: Overall, we find modest changes in intact tRNA capture following AlkB demethylation, with up to ~threefold altered levels of capture of a variety of tRNAs in the mouse system (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: AlkB treatment resulted in globally increased levels of the majority of 3′ tRNA halves.
source: Turning next to cloning of tRNA fragments, AlkB treatment resulted in globally increased levels of the majority of 3′ tRNA halves (Figure 5C and D), consistent with the m1A present at position 58 in the majority of tRNAs impeding reverse transcription.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The m1A present at position 58 in the majority of tRNAs impedes reverse transcription.
source: Turning next to cloning of tRNA fragments, AlkB treatment resulted in globally increased levels of the majority of 3′ tRNA halves (Figure 5C and D), consistent with the m1A present at position 58 in the majority of tRNAs impeding reverse transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased capture of 3' tRNA halves after AlkB treatment.

claim: The m22G modification interferes with reverse transcription by the OTTR RT enzyme.
source: Finally, as AlkB had no effect on m22G levels, we also cloned tRNA halves from a trm1Δ yeast strain – lacking this modification – overexpressing RNY1p. As with m1A, we find that the m22G modification interferes with reverse transcription by the OTTR RT enzyme, as we observed in our trm1Δ samples ~fourfold increased levels of those 5′ tRNA halves that normally carry this modification in wild-type (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5D showing increased capture in trm1Δ.

claim: Although OTTR can successfully clone modified tRNAs, cloning efficiency is nonetheless affected by m1A and m22G.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that although OTTR can successfully clone modified tRNAs, cloning efficiency is nonetheless affected by m1A and m22G.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AlkB and trm1Δ experiments.

claim: AlkB-mediated demethylation of m1A should be a routine addition to OTTR-based characterization of tRNA levels.
source: Although at present there is no enzymatic treatment commercially available to remove m22G, AlkB-mediated demethylation of m1A should be a routine addition to OTTR-based characterization of tRNA levels.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: OTTR performs comparably to the mim-tRNAseq method and the YAMAT-seq protocol for full-length tRNA cloning.
source: First, considering full-length tRNA cloning, OTTR performs comparably to the mim-tRNAseq method (Behrens et al., 2021), which ligates an adaptor to complete or partial RT products, and the YAMAT-seq protocol (Shigematsu et al., 2017), which ligates adaptors to mature tRNA acceptor stems before RT (Behrens et al., 2021; Shigematsu et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All three protocols (OTTR, mim-tRNAseq, YAMAT-seq) give some readout of diverse nucleotide modifications including m1G, m22G, m3C, m1A, i6A, t6A, inosine, and wybutosine, inferred from mismatches between sequencing read and genomic locus.
source: Although they use different RTs, all three protocols give some readout of diverse nucleotide modifications including m1G, m22G, m3C, m1A, i6A, t6A, inosine, and wybutosine, inferred from mismatches between sequencing read and genomic locus.
evidence: This is based on analysis of misincorporation patterns in the data.

claim: YAMAT-seq provides the most specific capture of intact tRNAs due to the ligation step involving a Y-shaped adaptor targeting the 3' CCA of mature tRNAs.
source: YAMAT-seq provides the most specific capture of intact tRNAs due to the ligation step involving a Y-shaped adaptor targeting the 3' CCA of mature tRNAs; subsequent PCR can only amplify full-length tRNAs.
evidence: This is based on understanding of the YAMAT-seq protocol design.

claim: YAMAT-seq libraries exhibit poor complexity, with the vast majority (82–86%) of tRNA sequences coming from two tRNA species.
source: However, YAMAT-seq libraries exhibit poor complexity, with the vast majority (82–86%) of tRNA sequences coming from two tRNA species.
evidence: This is based on analysis of YAMAT-seq data by the authors.

claim: mim-tRNAseq and OTTR exhibit similar levels of intact tRNA capture and similar complexity of species captured.
source: In contrast, mim-tRNAseq and OTTR exhibit similar levels of intact tRNA capture, similar complexity of species captured, with good (R~0.5) correlations between the protocols in measured tRNA levels in yeast (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), albeit with mim-tRNAseq exhibiting better (R~0.96) correlation than OTTR (R~0.7) to tRNA gene copy numbers.
evidence: This is based on comparison data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: OTTR more accurately captures tRNA fragments than NEBNext, Illumina TruSeq, an UMI-based custom protocol, and the recently developed PANDORA protocol.
source: We additionally show that OTTR more accurately captures tRNA fragments than NEBNext, Illumina TruSeq, an UMI-based custom protocol (Fu et al., 2018), and the recently developed PANDORA protocol (Shi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparison data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Among published mouse sperm datasets, only LIDAR exhibits similar complexity in tRF capture to OTTR.
source: Among published mouse sperm datasets, only LIDAR (Scacchetti et al., 2024) exhibits similar complexity in tRF capture to OTTR.
evidence: This is based on comparison data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: OTTR is suitable for cloning of both full-length tRNAs as well as tRNA fragments.
source: We demonstrate here that OTTR is suitable for cloning of both full-length tRNAs as well as tRNA fragments, in contrast to protocols such as YAMAT-seq which require adaptor ligation to the intact tRNA acceptor stem (Shigematsu et al., 2017) and are thus limited to full-length tRNA cloning.
evidence: This is demonstrated by data showing capture of both intact tRNAs and tRFs.

claim: The Nanopore-based nano-tRNAseq can capture full-length tRNAs, but the read numbers in the extant dataset are orders of magnitude lower than obtainable using short read sequencing.
source: Similarly, although the Nanopore-based nano-tRNAseq can capture full-length tRNAs, the read numbers in the extant dataset are orders of magnitude lower than obtainable using short read sequencing (~200–400,000 reads in the two datasets in the Supplement from Lucas et al., 2024), and the current protocol is not suitable for capturing shorter species like tRNA fragments.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published nano-tRNAseq data.

claim: OTTR is comparable to mim-tRNAseq in applicability.
source: In our view, OTTR is comparable to mim-tRNAseq (Behrens et al., 2021) in applicability: although mim-tRNAseq has not yet been benchmarked against tRNA fragments, the efficient capture of full-length tRNAs, along with the workflow that does not rely on specialized acceptor stem ligation, suggest that this protocol could perform similarly to OTTR for shorter RNAs.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment based on protocol characteristics.

claim: The use of random priming for LIDAR results in full-length tRNAs being captured as partial fragments.
source: LIDAR is also comparable, with advantages and disadvantages relative to OTTR and mim-tRNAseq: the use of random priming for LIDAR results in full-length tRNAs being captured as partial fragments, which makes this protocol a poor choice for applications focused on simultaneous capture of intact and fragmented tRNAs in the same sample.
evidence: This is based on understanding of the LIDAR protocol design.

claim: LIDAR can capture RNA species with blocked 3' ends, regardless of the nature of the 3' block.
source: On the other hand, the internal priming enables capture of RNA species with blocked 3' ends, regardless of the nature of the 3' block – while 3' phosphates can be resolved with PNK treatment, other 3' blocks may be novel or may lack appropriate treatments for resolution, and in these cases LIDAR (and Hydro-tRNAseq Gogakos et al., 2017) are uniquely suited to overcoming the blocked 3' end.
evidence: This is based on understanding of how LIDAR's random priming works.

claim: AlkB-mediated demethylation of various tRNA nucleotides results in significantly improved capture of 3′ tRNA halves.
source: We show here that AlkB-mediated demethylation of various tRNA nucleotides – as pioneered in the ARM-Seq and DM-Seq methods (Zheng et al., 2015; Cozen et al., 2015; Dai et al., 2017) – results in significantly improved capture of 3′ tRNA halves (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Eliminating m22G via deletion of Trm1 results in improved capture of relevant tRNA halves.
source: Moreover, eliminating m22G via deletion of Trm1 also results in improved capture of relevant tRNA halves (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: For tRNA or tRF quantification, it is recommended to carry out OTTR on AlkB-demethylated input RNAs.
source: Taken together, for tRNA or tRF quantification, we recommend carrying out OTTR on AlkB-demethylated input RNAs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Altered levels of tRNAs or tRNA halves in a given biological system could either reflect changes to tRNA production or stability, or could result from altered levels of inhibitory nucleotide modifications.
source: That said, modifications such as m22G cannot yet be easily removed; it is therefore essential to keep in mind that altered levels of tRNAs or tRNA halves in a given biological system could either reflect changes to tRNA production or stability, or could result from altered levels of inhibitory nucleotide modifications.
evidence: This is a cautionary note based on the findings about modification effects.

claim: The consensus view of mammalian sperm RNAs has been that they are dominated by 5′ tRFs, with 5′ ends of tRNA-Glu-CTC, Val-CAC, Val-AAC, Gly-GCC, and Gly-CCC being most abundant.
source: Over the past decade, scores of studies have largely agreed in defining the mammalian sperm small RNA payload as being dominated by 5′ tRFs, with 5′ ends of tRNA-Glu-CTC, Val-CAC, Val-AAC, Gly-GCC, and Gly-CCC being most abundant (Peng et al., 2012; Sharma, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the consensus from published literature.

claim: Removal of 3′ phosphate or 2′–3′ cyclic phosphate modifications revealed a large population of rRNA fragments, as well as slightly longer 5′ tRNA fragments than typically captured.
source: We previously showed that removal of 3′ phosphate or 2′–3′ cyclic phosphate modifications revealed a large population of rRNA fragments, as well as slightly longer 5′ tRNA fragments than typically captured, consistent with RNase A or T family cleavage events being responsible for rRNA and tRNA cleavage in the germline (Sharma et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: RNase A or T family cleavage events are responsible for rRNA and tRNA cleavage in the germline.
source: We previously showed that removal of 3′ phosphate or 2′–3′ cyclic phosphate modifications revealed a large population of rRNA fragments, as well as slightly longer 5′ tRNA fragments than typically captured, consistent with RNase A or T family cleavage events being responsible for rRNA and tRNA cleavage in the germline (Sharma et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of PNK treatment on RNA capture.

claim: Using OTTR provides the most accurate picture of the sperm small RNA payload to date.
source: Here, we build on these studies, using OTTR to provide the most accurate picture of the sperm small RNA payload to date.
evidence: This is the authors' claim based on their OTTR data.

claim: Sperm carry a population of small RNAs dominated by rRNA fragments, along with both 5′ and 3′ tRNA halves arising from the majority of tRNAs.
source: We find that sperm carry a population of small RNAs dominated by rRNA fragments, along with both 5′ and 3′ tRNA halves arising from the majority of tRNAs.
evidence: This is based on OTTR sequencing data from mouse sperm.

claim: Smaller populations of microRNAs and piRNAs are present in sperm, consistent with prior reports of the sperm RNA payload.
source: Smaller populations of microRNAs and piRNAs are also present, consistent with prior reports of the sperm RNA payload.
evidence: This is based on OTTR data and comparison to published literature.

claim: The revised view of sperm small RNAs is more consistent with a generalized cleavage of the RNA populations of any typical cell.
source: Instead, our revised view of sperm small RNAs is more consistent with a generalized cleavage of the RNA populations of any typical cell, with the preponderance of rRNA and tRNA fragments consistent with the abundance of the intact precursor species in developing sperm or typical somatic tissues.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The data motivate a reappraisal of the biogenesis of structural RNA fragments in the male germline.
source: Our data do not address the question of whether a given rRNA or tRNA fragment derives from 'in situ' cleavage of rRNAs or tRNAs present at the completion of spermatogenesis – as opposed to their being generated in somatic support cells in the reproductive tract (Conine and Rando, 2022) – but our data motivate a reappraisal of the biogenesis of structural RNA fragments in the male germline.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the implications of their findings.

claim: Given that for many tRNAs both 5′ and 3′ tRNA halves can be found in sperm at similar abundance, it will be important to understand the biochemical context in which these RNAs are delivered to the zygote.
source: However, given our finding that for many tRNAs both 5′ and 3′ tRNA halves can be found in sperm at similar abundance, it will be important to understand the biochemical context in which these RNAs are delivered to the zygote.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the implications of their findings.

claim: Understanding the molecular nature of the tRNA halves that are delivered to the zygote during fertilization has major implications for their potential functions in the early embryo.
source: Understanding the molecular nature of the tRNA halves that are delivered to the zygote during fertilization has major implications for their potential functions in the early embryo.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the implications of their findings.

claim: The data significantly update our understanding of the sperm epigenome.
source: Together, our data significantly update our understanding of the sperm epigenome, and motivate re-appraisal of mammalian germline small RNA biogenesis, and of stress and diet effects on sperm RNA populations.
evidence: This is the authors' summary of the impact of their findings.
